title: Call for police to investigate Scottish hospital after 19 deaths due to surgery
text:
A senior surgeon has called for a criminal investigation into a Scottish hospital after it emerged that at least 19 patients had died from avoidable complications due to surgery.
Dr Mohammed Habib, a consultant at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, said he had repeatedly reported concerns about the hospital’s liver and pancreatic surgery from 2021 onwards and believed dozens of patients may have died unnecessarily there.
Calling for a police investigation into corporate homicide at the hospital, Habib alleged that senior officials at NHS Grampian, the crisis-hit health board which runs it, failed to take the correct action quickly enough.
Habib said NHS Grampian eventually commissioned an expert report to investigate his allegations, and those from a second whistleblower, which confirmed his allegations that 19 patients had died due to “serious adverse events” caused by surgery between 2015 and 2021.
Their internal report was published on Thursday by Habib’s solicitor, Aamer Anwar.
Habib’s comments and the findings were discussed in Holyrood later on Thursday. John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, said Habib’s disclosures were “of the gravest concern”. The NHS had legal duties to give patients the best possible care and to quickly investigate allegations about safety failures, he said.
But he rebuffed demands from Michael Marra, the Scottish Labour leader, for a criminal investigation into the “systemic failures” at NHS Grampian.
Speaking at first minister’s questions, Marra said the families of the 19 people who died “deserve answers and deserve justice”.
Swinney denied that the government had ignored Habib’s complaints and said the recent decision to demand changes of leadership and urgent reforms at the board should produce the necessary improvements.
Laura Skaife-Knight, the chief executive of NHS Grampian, said: “We are aware of the serious allegations raised today. A thorough investigation has already taken place into these matters, with some elements of that work ongoing. Any new evidence or information will be carefully considered, and NHS Grampian will continue to respond through the appropriate clinical, governance and legal processes.
“We understand the allegations will cause further concern to patients, members of the public and staff. It is important we respect patient and employee confidentiality, but we can highlight that where reviews identify issues around patient care, the appropriate duty of candour processes are followed. This includes direct communication with patients and families where required.
“If our consideration of any new evidence identifies further individuals who should be contacted, we will do so. Patient safety remains our highest priority.”
The two external experts who carried out the review in 2022, surgery professors at Edinburgh and Leeds universities, concluded the “extremely high” death rate at Aberdeen between 2017 and 2020 ran as high as 18% within liver and pancreatic surgery.
It said the national average for surgery-related fatalities was 2-3% for that speciality, depending on the patient’s condition.
Habib, who still works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, said the unit continued operating on patients. He then flagged the cases of four other patients who had died during or after surgery since that expert report was completed.
In March 2026, another external expert said it was imperative that surgery ended there, telling hospital executives its “persistent high mortality in complex surgery is a red-flag indicator of systemic failure”. The liver and pancreatic surgery department was then shut down.
Based on the fatality calculations made in 2022, Habib said dozens of patients may have died unnecessarily at the hospital.
He said he had repeatedly contacted the police, Scottish government ministers and Scotland’s independent whistleblowing officer, but was fobbed off, or told the cases he raised were time-barred.
His allegations are the latest in a series of medical and managerial crises at NHS Grampian, which have led to paediatric surgery at Gray’s hospital being shut down, the replacement of the board’s chairperson and its medical director, and independent investigations into other serious adverse events at its hospitals.
Last week, Angela Constance, the Scottish health secretary, told MSPs there were extremely serious systemic problems with mismanagement and underperformance at NHS Grampian.
In a statement at Holyrood, she told MSPs the health board faced being put into special measures if its current reforms were not introduced quickly or effectively enough.
Last week, a report by Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS), an NHS watchdog, found “very serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian’s leadership”, which included failing to be transparent and accurate in its accounts of its actions.
There had been “persistent, serious concerns about safety, quality, clinical governance and leadership” at the board, it said.
However, the HIS report only identified one patient death due to a serious adverse event.
Habib and Anwar said the evidence from the expert review into Habib’s unit had shown many more deaths were avoidable, and that this raised their concerns about whether the full extent of the crisis at NHS Grampian was being covered up.
Habib said NHS Grampian was “avoiding accountability by not being transparent about what damage has been done, while promising heaven and earth going forward.
“In every other death at the hands of the state, families would be entitled to understand the circumstances of their loved ones’ death. [They] deserve to know how and why their loved one died.”
Anwar said the lord advocate, Ruth Charteris KC, should instruct her lawyers and Police Scotland to launch a criminal investigation. Ministers should immediately place NHS Grampian into special measures, he added.
There was a “catastrophic failure to act” at NHS Grampian, Anwar said. “While the Grampian leadership was busy burying evidence behind complex medical jargon, they also failed to explain to bereaved families that their loved ones had died after the wrong operation.”
A Scottish government spokesperson said: “We recognise the courage shown by this whistleblower to raise concerns. Everyone who works in our NHS should feel safe and supported to speak up without fear of detriment.
“Ministers have already committed to transparently setting out all engagement with NHS Grampian in relation to the concerns raised in the HIS review.
“The government took action and repeatedly raised the concerns of Dr Habib with both Healthcare Improvement Scotland and NHS Grampian. As the HIS review set out last week, there were clear failures in the former medical leadership and in how concerns were being addressed within NHS Grampian.
“NHS Grampian is now subject to a very significant level of intervention and an unprecedented level of support.
“Any criminal investigation is a matter for Police Scotland.”
Police Scotland has been approached for comment.
